title: Bayes' theorem and the independence assumption
lesson: Naive Bayes assumes features are independent given the class. On this data 4 of 5 tested pairs violate that assumption materially — passenger class and fare band are near-deterministic in each other. The classifier still reaches ROC-AUC 0.837 against 0.844 for logistic regression, which makes no such assumption. The reason is that ranking depends only on the *ordering* of posteriors, and dependence tends to distort their magnitudes more than their order. That is also why Naive Bayes probabilities should not be trusted as probabilities: its Brier score is 0.1561 against 0.1446.

quiz.question: Naive Bayes assumes P(A,B|C) = P(A|C)·P(B|C). On this data, Pclass and FareBand are strongly dependent given survival. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The classifier's ranking collapses to random
Predicted probabilities become over-confident, but ranking largely survives
The model cannot be fitted at all
Nothing — the assumption is only needed for training speed
quiz.explanation: Dependent features contribute correlated evidence that the model counts as though it were independent, so posteriors are pushed toward 0 and 1. Ordering is largely preserved, which is why ROC-AUC stays respectable while the Brier score degrades.

quiz.question: The prior P(survived) is 0.384. A passenger is female in first class. Which quantity does Bayes' theorem use to convert that evidence into a posterior?
options: The likelihood P(evidence | survived) and the marginal P(evidence)
quiz.explanation: Posterior ∝ prior × likelihood. The marginal P(evidence) normalises so the posteriors across classes sum to one.
